slots.practicalActivity: Write one paragraph describing a real or representative incident where bad data caused a specific business problem (a wrong report, a missed shipment, a failed reconciliation); then name which one or two of the six quality dimensions (accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity, uniqueness, timeliness) the incident actually violated.
slots.deliverable: A short written incident description with the violated quality dimension(s) explicitly named.

slots.practicalActivity: For the incident from the previous slot, name who should own fixing it (a data steward, a source-system owner, a BI developer) and why; then map the incident onto the data quality lifecycle stages (profile, define rules, assess, remediate, monitor) by naming which stage was missing or broke down.
slots.deliverable: A short written note naming the responsible role and the specific lifecycle stage that failed for your incident.

slots.practicalActivity: In SSMS, connect to a local AdventureWorks or Northwind instance (or any SQL Server database you have), open a New Query window, and write a COUNT(*) / COUNT(DISTINCT ...) query against a table with a supposed primary identifier column; then extend it to profile the NULL rate of two more columns using the SUM(CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) pattern, converting one result to a percentage with 100.0 * ... / COUNT(*).
slots.deliverable: A screenshot or saved .sql file with the row-count/distinct-count query and the NULL-rate percentage query, both run against a real table.

slots.practicalActivity: On the same database, profile one text column's value distribution (min/max length, distinct value list if small, or a GROUP BY count of the most common values) to spot inconsistent casing or formatting; then write a pattern-profiling query (e.g., LIKE or a format check) that flags rows where a column (phone, email, or postal code) doesn't match the expected pattern.
slots.deliverable: Two SQL profiling queries: one column/value-distribution query and one pattern-matching query flagging malformed values, with their results.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the profiling results from the previous two slots and write a short profiling summary: which columns are genuinely risky versus which null/pattern results are explainable and acceptable, and what you'd prioritize investigating first.
slots.deliverable: A short written profiling summary prioritizing the riskiest finding from your own profiling queries.

slots.practicalActivity: Create (or use existing) a small reference table and a current table with a shared key, and write a query joining them to flag rows where a compared column disagrees (an accuracy check); then write a completeness query computing the NULL percentage of a required field, converted to a percentage with CAST(... AS DECIMAL(5,2)).
slots.deliverable: One accuracy-check query (joined against a reference table) and one completeness-check query (NULL percentage), both run with real results.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a consistency check comparing how the same fact is represented across two columns or tables that should agree (e.g., status codes stored differently in two systems); then write a validity check using a CHECK-style WHERE clause that flags rows violating a rule about allowed values, data type, or range (e.g., a status column outside its allowed list, or a date in the future).
slots.deliverable: One consistency-check query and one validity-check query, each returning the specific rows that fail.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a uniqueness check using GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to find duplicate records on a key that should be unique; then write a timeliness check comparing a record's last-updated timestamp against the current date to flag records older than an agreed freshness threshold (e.g., stale more than 30 days).
slots.deliverable: One duplicate-finding uniqueness query and one staleness-flagging timeliness query, each with real results from your database.

slots.practicalActivity: Write three formal data quality rules (ID, plain-language statement, and the dimension each belongs to) for a table of your choice, modeled on the course's ORD-002/CUST-004/INV-001 style; then implement all three as SQL checks and combine them into one UNION ALL failures report with RuleName and RecordKey columns, following the 'write the WHERE clause for the failure' pattern.
slots.deliverable: Three documented data quality rules plus one combined UNION ALL failures-report query implementing all three, with results.

slots.practicalActivity: Create two small test tables with a parent/child relationship including at least one orphaned child row, write the LEFT JOIN ... WHERE ... IS NULL query to find it, and add it as a fourth branch to your failures report; then sketch (in writing) a cross-system reconciliation check comparing a total (row count or sum) between two systems that are supposed to agree.
slots.deliverable: An extended failures-report query including a referential integrity branch, plus a written reconciliation-check design comparing two systems' totals.

slots.practicalActivity: Write explicit pass/warn/fail thresholds (e.g., On track if pass rate >= 98%, At risk 95-98%, Behind below 95%) for two of your rules from this chapter; then sketch how you'd automate the failures-report query to run on a schedule (SQL Server Agent job, or a scripted task) and where its output should land for someone to review.
slots.deliverable: Written thresholds for two rules, plus a short automation plan naming the scheduling mechanism and the output destination.

slots.practicalActivity: Rules-and-checks lab: build one consolidated UNION ALL failures report combining at least five distinct checks from this chapter (spanning at least three different quality dimensions and including one referential integrity check), each with a RuleName label and a SARGable WHERE clause, and run it against your own test or sample database end to end.
slots.deliverable: One complete SQL script producing a single failures report with at least five labeled rule checks across three or more dimensions, with real run results.

slots.practicalActivity: Take one failure from your Chapter 4 failures report and run a 5 Whys chain on it (five numbered questions and answers) to reach a root cause, sorting it into people/process/technology/source data; then write the cleansing or standardization fix for the existing bad rows, separate from the root-cause fix for new rows going forward.
slots.deliverable: A written 5 Whys chain ending in a categorized root cause, plus a separate cleansing/standardization fix statement for existing bad rows.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch a remediation workflow (detect -> triage -> assign -> fix -> verify) for the root cause from the previous slot, naming who does each step; then design a monitoring query that logs your chosen rule's daily pass rate (total checked vs. total failed) so the trend can be tracked over time instead of checked once.
slots.deliverable: A written remediation workflow with named steps/owners, plus a monitoring query that logs a daily pass-rate figure for one rule.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch a simple scorecard for three of your rules (current value, target, status, owner, one row per metric), using the thresholds from Chapter 4; then design a lightweight issue-tracking log (columns: issue, rule, root cause, owner, status, date opened/closed) and populate it with one real entry from this course's work.
slots.deliverable: A sketched three-metric scorecard (value/target/status/owner), plus one populated row in an issue-tracking log.

lessons.title: Data Quality Case Study: Customer Data
Data Quality Case Study: Financial Data

slots.practicalActivity: Following the profile-diagnose-remediate-monitor structure from the customer-data case study, write your own one-paragraph walkthrough for a different fictional scenario of mismatched customer loyalty-tier values across two systems (naming which dimensions it touches and a standardization fix); then, in the same structure, sketch a financial-data scenario (e.g., mismatched transaction totals between a source ledger and a reporting table) and name the one profiling query you'd run first to confirm its scale.
slots.deliverable: Two short written case-study walkthroughs (customer and financial), each naming the dimensions involved and a first profiling query or fix.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone review: write a two-page data quality management plan for a real or realistic dataset of your choosing -- the quality dimensions most at risk, three formal rules with their SQL checks combined into one failures report, a root-cause-to-remediation workflow for one real finding, a monitoring/scorecard design with thresholds, and an issue-management log entry demonstrating the finding being tracked to resolution.
slots.deliverable: A two-page written data quality management plan covering dimensions, rules/checks, remediation workflow, monitoring/scorecard, and one tracked issue log entry.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can profile a real SQL Server table end to end, write and combine SQL data quality checks across all six dimensions into a single failures report, run a root-cause analysis instead of just cleaning symptoms, and design the monitoring, scorecard, and issue-tracking layer that keeps a fix from recurring -- the measurable, SQL-grounded quality practice the rest of the Data Governance Engineer path builds its policies and stewardship on.
